hero.headline: Vero Beach group collects donations for Venezuela earthquake victims through Saturday
hero.teaser: Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach is collecting essential supplies to ship directly to communities devastated by a massive earthquake in Venezuela.
hero.body:
Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach is hosting a Venezuela Earthquake Relief Drive, collecting essential supplies to ship directly to those affected by a massive earthquake. The drive is being organized by founders Lourana Navarro and Juliana Marino, along with Heidi Ramirez. Navarro, who was born in Venezuela and now lives in Vero Beach, said her family in Caracas is safe, but surrounding communities have lost everything. The earthquake measured 7.5 in magnitude.

The organizers are working with Global Empowerment Mission to ship collected supplies to Venezuela, and say 100% of donated supplies will be directed through verified humanitarian relief efforts. Marino said hundreds of thousands of people are in need right now. Navarro said the worst needs are food and places to sleep and bathe. She said the scale of destruction will take decades to address and Venezuela does not have the resources to recover.

Donations can be dropped off at 684 Old Dixie Hwy, Vero Beach. The collection runs through Saturday, June 27, 2026, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The organizers are collecting items including powder Gatorade, non-perishable food, baby formula and food, diapers, baby wipes, feminine hygiene products, soap, shampoo, toothbrushes and toothpaste, blankets, sleeping bags, flashlights with batteries, first aid kits, bandages, hand sanitizer, cleaning supplies, face masks, nitrile gloves, and plastic bins with lids. To reach the organizers, contact Lourana Navarro at (954) 205-0700, Juliana Marino at (772) 913-0805, or Heidi Ramirez at (772) 213-2747.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis signs updated Live Local Act to expand affordable housing across Florida
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis has signed the newest version of the Live Local Act, legislation that has now been revised three times since its original approval three years ago. Senate bill SB 962, sponsored by Green Cove Springs Republican Sen. Jennifer Bradley, and House bill HB 837, sponsored by Coral Gables Republican Rep., both passed the Florida House and Senate this month. The updated law continues efforts to address Florida's housing shortage by expanding affordable residential options while limiting local government control over housing development.

The revised legislation requires cities and counties to permit apartment buildings and mixed-use housing projects in areas currently zoned for commercial or industrial purposes, provided that at least 40% of the units are designated as affordable housing for a 30-year period. This requirement can also apply to land owned by local governments, school districts, and large religious institutions. The law restricts how much local governments can control the height and design of these developments, making it more difficult for cities and counties to prevent projects through zoning restrictions. The measure will expand the types of dwelling units allowed, reduce local limitations on development, and protect funding sources for home purchases. Agricultural land and farm operations remain excluded from these provisions.

The original Live Local Act faced criticism from organizations like Florida TaxWatch for not going far enough to help middle-income renters. This group identified a gap in the housing market for households earning too much to qualify for affordable housing subsidies but too little to afford market-rate rents in their communities. In August, TaxWatch published a report recommending that legislators revisit and strengthen the measure. The state responded by enacting these revisions, which address some of the shortcomings identified in the watchdog group's analysis.

The updated Live Local Act represents a significant shift in Florida's approach to its housing crisis. By reducing local control over development design and height while requiring acceptance of affordable housing projects in commercial and industrial zones, the state has taken a stronger position in removing construction barriers. The mandate that 40% of units remain affordable for three decades establishes a long-term commitment to preserving housing accessible to lower-income Floridians. The original measure from 2023 aimed to increase affordable and workforce housing construction through funding mechanisms, tax incentives, and zoning changes. These latest updates build on that foundation with more aggressive state-level intervention in local land-use decisions.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets game postponed Saturday, rescheduled for late July in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: The St.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets game against the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels scheduled for Saturday was postponed. The game will be rescheduled for late July in Port St. Lucie.

The postponement came after the Mighty Mussels defeated the Mets 6-2 earlier in the series, hitting four home runs in that contest. The teams had been playing a series that included games in Fort Myers.

The rescheduled game will take place at the Mets' home ballpark in Port St. Lucie later in the season. The exact date in late July has been set but specific scheduling details were announced through MLB.com.

The St. Lucie Mets continue their Florida State League season with the makeup game to be added to the Port St. Lucie schedule. Fans who purchased tickets for the postponed Saturday game will need to check with the team regarding ticket policies for the rescheduled contest.

cards.headline: Florida Republicans rally at Hard Rock Hotel with August primaries approaching
cards.teaser: Florida Republicans gathered at the Hard Rock Hotel for a rally ahead of the August primaries, with affordability, property tax reform and overdevelopment emerging as top voter concerns.
cards.body:
Florida Republicans gathered at the Hard Rock Hotel for a rally ahead of the August primaries, drawing Sen. Rick Scott and candidates for governor as the party worked to energize its base. Affordability emerged as a top concern among voters, with attendee Jessica Johnson calling it "the main issue" facing Florida residents. Johnson also emphasized the importance of responsible development, noting that once land is developed, "you can't undo it." Voter Rhonda Lopez defended property tax relief proposals against arguments that such measures would harm public services, saying the government needs to "tighten its belt, just like the working man has to."

Political analyst Susan McManus noted speakers conveyed a clear message that Republicans cannot take the election for granted. She identified major themes throughout the event including affordability broken into home insurance and tax issues, law enforcement, and education, with children's safety, their future, and parents' rights serving as an overarching theme. McManus said the governor and attorney general races warrant close attention. For 18-year-old first-time voter Grant Mandel of Boca Raton, the event marked his entry into politics. McManus warned that 30 percent of Floridians unregistered with either party represent "a huge unknown" in the upcoming elections and that time is running short for candidates seeking the nomination.

cards.headline: Two killed in head-on crash on Allapattah Road in Martin County
cards.teaser: Two people died in a head-on collision on Allapattah Road in Martin County on Saturday.
cards.body:
Two people died in a head-on collision on Allapattah Road in Martin County on Saturday. The crash was described as horrific by officials responding to the scene.

The fatal collision occurred Saturday evening on Allapattah Road. Both drivers were killed in the impact.

Authorities responded to the crash scene on Allapattah Road. The investigation into the circumstances of the head-on collision is ongoing.

The double fatality marks a serious traffic incident for Martin County. Allapattah Road was affected by the crash response and investigation.

hero.headline: 2 people killed in head-on crash on Allapattah Road in Indiantown
hero.teaser: Two people died in a head-on crash along Allapattah Road near Martin Highway in Indiantown on Saturday morning.
hero.body:
The crash occurred around 6:30 a.m. at 8113 SW Allapattah Road, also known as the Allapattah S-Curve, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Two people were killed in the head-on collision.

Allapattah Road was blocked for about 6 hours Saturday morning while the Florida Highway Patrol processed the scene. The road has since reopened.

cards.headline: Missing diver found dead off Fort Pierce in 55 feet of water
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is investigating after a missing diver was found dead on the ocean floor approximately 6 to 7 miles north-northeast of the Fort Pierce Inlet. The U.S. Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed 4 vessels to assist in the search. The FWC also contacted the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit, which had independently monitored the Mayday call and was already en route to assist. A group of civilian boaters who were friends of the missing diver departed the Fort Pierce Inlet at approximately 1 p.m. Aerial support was provided by both the Coast Guard and FWC.

At approximately 4:10 p.m., civilian divers entered the water and located the missing diver at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. Martin County Fire Rescue Lieutenant Daniel DeGrazia recovered the diver from the ocean floor. The diver was pronounced dead at the scene and transported to Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division is conducting an ongoing investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident. The victim's name was expected to be released Monday.

cards.headline: West Boca Raton homeowner battles delays in receiving My Safe Florida Home grant after completing work
cards.body:
Anne Bendel of West Boca Raton first contacted WPTV in May about her My Safe Florida Home grant application being held up by missing paperwork from her insurance company. After that issue was resolved, program representatives told her in May that her status was complete. One week later, My Safe Florida Home requested additional documentation, specifically a permit of completion for a large impact window. When Bendel provided the permit, representatives raised questions about dates on the paperwork. Her application is now back under review as she waits to learn whether she will receive any reimbursement for the $8,000 she paid out of pocket for the work.

Bendel describes herself as persistent and thorough but says the grant process has pushed her to her limits. "I don't have a computer, I'm doing this on my phone, and I have nobody to help me. It's gut-wrenching," she said. She believes the program is not treating her fairly, noting that she completed all required work, obtained necessary permits, and provided requested insurance documentation. The My Safe Florida Home program offers grants of up to $10,000 to help homeowners fortify their homes against storms and earn insurance discounts. WPTV has contacted the Florida Department of Financial Services in Tallahassee regarding Bendel's case and the status of her grant application.

hero.headline: Florida Highwaymen Museum in Fort Pierce featured in America 250 Road Trip
hero.teaser: The Florida Highwaymen Museum at 1234 Avenue D in Fort Pierce has been selected as a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip celebrating the nation's 250th birthday.
hero.body:
The city of Fort Pierce announced on its Facebook page this week that the Florida Highwaymen Museum is part of the America 250 festivities. The museum opened this year and is the nation's only one with exhibitions that include paintings from each of the 26 renowned Highwaymen artists.

The museum celebrates 26 Black artists who began painting in the 1950s, creating bold, colorful landscapes of Florida's untouched beauty and selling them along the roadside when segregation kept them out of traditional galleries. The museum is located at 1234 Avenue D in Fort Pierce.

During the summer from June 16 through July 31, the museum is open Saturday and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m. The museum will be closed in August and reopen in September with a new exhibit. Fall and spring hours from September 1 through June 15 will be expanded.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. after facility closure
cards.teaser: Following the closure of Alligator Alcatraz in the Florida Everglades, detainees have been moved to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and Washington state, creating challenges for families and immigration attorneys.
cards.body:
Immigration attorney Richard Hujber said detainees from the now-closed Alligator Alcatraz facility have been scattered across the country, with clients relocated to Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. According to Hujber, these relocations create significant legal challenges when fighting for bonds and navigating immigration law, as different circuit courts in different parts of the country apply different standards. With bond now out of reach for some detainees, Hujber says they face difficult decisions about whether to continue pursuing residency or asylum or to self-deport instead.

Gov. Ron DeSantis reported that roughly 21,000 people have been deported from the facility since it opened nearly a year ago. For some families, the facility's closure brought relief. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before Alligator Alcatraz shut down and is now under an order of supervision, which allows him to drive, work and live in the U.S. However, the Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational, and for many former detainees and their families, the future remains uncertain.

hero.headline: SoFlo Market brings patriotic celebration to Boca Raton City Hall July 4
hero.teaser: The popular SoFlo Market will turn Boca Raton City Hall into a hub of red, white and blue celebration this Independence Day with a free monthly event drawing families and local shopping enthusiasts from across Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
The SoFlo Market will take place Saturday, July 4, at Boca Raton City Hall, drawing families, food lovers and local shopping enthusiasts from across Palm Beach County. Founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas told WPTV the market's mission is to uplift small local businesses and bring the community together. For the holiday, organizers are adding extra patriotic flair. Highlights include a kids parade, a DJ, unique vendors, gourmet food and the first 20 children through the gate receiving a free gift.

Visitors can expect face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf, and balloon twisting, alongside the market's signature array of handmade crafts and mouthwatering desserts. A live appearance by the SoFlo Market's flamboyant flamingo mascot is set to be a crowd favorite. Boca Raton firefighters and police officers have been invited to share the day with residents, reinforcing the family-first atmosphere.

Kyle, Freitas' son, and Eddie, her husband, are part of the organizing team ensuring activities run smoothly. Electricity will be powered by generators on-site, and strong cell service means friends and family can share moments instantly across social media. The SoFlo Market runs monthly, but Freitas says the Independence Day edition is always a standout. The event takes place Saturday, July 4, 2026, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at Boca Raton City Hall, 201 West Palmetto Park Road. Admission is free.

cards.headline: Florida Mango Festival in West Palm Beach showcases 75 vendors, rare varieties this Saturday
cards.teaser: Florida-grown mangoes from sweet and creamy to citrusy and tropical will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beac.
cards.body:
Florida-grown mangoes will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center. The event will feature more than 75 vendors serving local mango varieties, grafted trees, tropical fruits, and mango-themed products. According to Alex Salazar of Tropical Acres Farms, the indoor, air-conditioned venue offers an ideal setting for people to taste, learn, and discover Florida-grown mangoes without worrying about summer heat. Festival co-organizer Vince Rogers previewed unique varieties including Fruit Cocktail, a sweet multi-layered flavor; Orange Sherbet, offering creamy citrus notes; and Pineapple Pleasure, with tropical pineapple undertones. Florida hosts more than 350 mango varieties far beyond what's typically available in grocery stores, Rogers said.

Throughout the day, visitors can attend educational talks on home mango growing and grafting techniques. Salazar will lead demonstrations offering tips for both beginners and seasoned growers. Additional features include an "ID Your Mango" booth, a scion exchange for online mango community members, and a master display of Florida's diverse mango cultivars. The festival takes place Saturday, June 27, 2026, at 10:30 a.m. at the Palm Beach County Convention Center, 650 Okeechobee Blvd., West Palm Beach. First pick ticket holders can enter at 9 a.m. Garage parking is included with tickets, with limited availability. Tickets and more information are available at floridamangofestival.com.

cards.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League urges South Florida pet owners to prepare hurricane plans
cards.teaser: With hurricane season in full swing, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits.
cards.body:
Dr. Alyssa Comroe, CEO of Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League, told WPTV that the safest place for pets during a hurricane is alongside their owners. The shelter's expert team recommends pet owners ensure their animals wear collars with current identification and have updated microchips registered with correct contact information. Owners should also introduce pets to a designated safe room ahead of time, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom, and conduct practice runs so the hurricane is not their first time there.

Pet owners should prepare an emergency kit containing a three-day supply of food and water in airtight containers, bowls, a sturdy carrier, bedding, towels, medications for two weeks, vaccination records, first-aid supplies, litter and box for cats, leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible ID. The shelter recommends keeping a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels in an accessible place and maintaining recent photos of pets, ideally with their owner, to help with identification if separated. Florida's hurricane season runs from June through November, overlapping with extreme summer heat. Proper storm preparation reduces risk during evacuations, while heat safety measures such as water enrichment, shade, and limiting midday walks help protect pets year-round.

cards.headline: Boca Raton's George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, has achieved a record-breaking milestone in 2026, awarding more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, distributed more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, according to President Tim Snow. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has now distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. The program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

GSSF's services extend beyond financial assistance. Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted the organization provides mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast. The Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, offers professional, formal, and casual wear so scholars can prepare for interviews, internships, and campus life. The boutique accepts donations of new or gently used clothing, footwear, and accessories. Recipient Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship, and plans to attend Georgetown University.

cards.headline: Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody assists earthquake relief efforts for Venezuela from Doral
cards.teaser: Attorney General Ashley Moody joined volunteers in Doral Saturday to help pack containers of food and relief supplies for Venezuela as thousands remain missing after devastating earthquakes.
cards.body:
Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody assisted earthquake relief efforts for Venezuela on Saturday at a staging area for the Global Empowerment Mission in Doral. Moody and her husband Justin helped pack containers of food and other boxes of relief supplies destined for areas devastated by earthquakes that struck Venezuela on Wednesday. "Florida stands with the Venezuelan people. Justin and I were inspired by the dedicated and passionate volunteers that gathered to donate and assemble aid for the Venezuelan people reeling from the devastating earthquakes," Moody said in a news release. She added that her office would continue to stand ready to assist those in need of help following the tragedy.

The Global Empowerment Mission, founded in Doral, remains at the forefront of international humanitarian relief efforts and specializes in rapid relief for disaster victims and long-term recovery assistance for natural disasters and humanitarian crises. The situation in Venezuela remains critical as thousands of people remain missing following back-to-back earthquakes. About 1,000 people have been confirmed dead, while another 50,000 are believed to still be missing. On Friday night, Venezuelan authorities blocked off access to La Guaira, the epicenter of destruction, as chaos and traffic affected search efforts. Citizens digging through rubble reported seeing few state rescue teams in the hardest-hit areas after the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes.

cards.headline: Florida resilience expert says disaster preparedness is state's best insurance policy
cards.teaser: On National Insurance Awareness Day, a Florida disaster resilience leader argues that strengthening homes and investing in mitigation creates a safer and more insurable Florida.
cards.body:
Leslie Chapman-Henderson, president and CEO of the Federal Alliance for Safe Homes, said National Insurance Awareness Day on June 28 offers an opportunity to discuss resilience as a critical insurance component. Drawing on 12 years in the insurance industry responding to catastrophes and 28 years advancing disaster resilience, Chapman-Henderson distinguishes between insurance and resilience: insurance helps people recover after disasters, while resilience helps them withstand disasters in the first place.

Florida has faced significant insurance challenges for decades due to frequent hurricanes, inflation, litigation costs and continued population growth in vulnerable areas. Following Hurricane Andrew in 1992, Florida strengthened its building codes, and today the state's high-wind standards rank among the nation's strongest. The state created My Safe Florida Home, the nation's first wind-mitigation grant program, which has invested more than $500 million to help thousands of homeowners strengthen their properties. Chapman-Henderson noted that homes built or upgraded to modern standards perform better during disasters and communities prioritizing preparedness recover faster. Researchers at Florida International University and the University of Florida, working with insurance industry engineers, continue developing innovations to protect lives and property while supporting a healthier insurance marketplace.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis praised World Cup visitors while critics note his own divisive rhetoric
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis praised the World Cup for giving visiting fans a chance to see America directly, but critics point to his own rhetoric painting internal enemies as destroying the country.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis praised World Cup visitors for seeing America as a good country, telling an audience "I wouldn't want to be anywhere else" and noting that visitors have witnessed both the generosity of Americans and that "this is a good country." However, observers point out that DeSantis, like many leaders, bears responsibility for painting a grim picture that fuels negative views of the country. DeSantis's political brand, which secured his election twice, launched a presidential campaign, and made him one of the most influential governors in the country, is substantially built on the premise that a vast, organized internal enemy is destroying the country. Teachers and school administrators who discussed gender identity in classrooms were called "groomers." Corporate executives supporting diversity programs were described as carriers of the "woke mind virus." California was depicted as "a civilization in decay leading an attack on the American family."

The World Cup has created what American political culture rarely produces intentionally: a setting where people from different countries interact with actual Americans and discover their preconceptions wrong. Fans from Scotland, Iran, Brazil, Morocco, and Australia arrived with impressions shaped by their own politics and media, but found something different. DeSantis acknowledged that visitors are recognizing "this is a good country," raising the question: "when the people who govern it are going to start acting like they believe the same thing."

cards.headline: Largo opens new City Hall and Pride Month draws debate at commission meeting
cards.teaser: Largo Mayor Woody Brown read a Pride Month proclamation at the June 2 Commission meeting after the city had planned to drop it from the agenda before residents objected.
cards.body:
Largo Mayor Woody Brown opened the June 2 Commission meeting by reading a Pride Month proclamation, a gesture the city had planned to drop from the agenda entirely before dozens of residents showed up to object. Many attendees arrived directly from the ribbon-cutting for Horizon West Bay, the $85 million mixed-use development anchored by the city's new City Hall. Brown explained in a June 1 online chat with residents that new legislation barring local governments from spending on diversity, equity and inclusion-related events and initiatives doesn't technically take effect until January. However, with the budget still unsigned, Brown said the Governor could still cut off funding streams Largo depends on, including dollars for stormwater infrastructure.

The same Commission recently passed an ordinance creating a new open-container entertainment district in the blocks surrounding the building, a program called Sip and Stroll that lets patrons walk freely through designated downtown zones with drinks purchased from approved local businesses. Abner Morales, who owns Wepaa Puerto Rican Restaurant nearby, is already designing custom branded cups. "That's awesome because we have like 16 employees. We want to keep running this business," he said. One Cozy Smoke Shop employee told Fox 13 she sees the district becoming almost like Bourbon Street in New Orleans.

cards.headline: Trump presidency raises questions about concentrated power ahead of America's 250th anniversary
cards.teaser: As the 250th anniversary of America's liberation from a king approaches, President Donald Trump's second term has led to comparisons with monarchical rule and debates over executive power.
cards.body:
The 250th anniversary of America's liberation from a king began with a campaign-style rally on the National Mall by President Donald Trump, whose face adorns banners across federal buildings in the nation's capital. Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has nominated one of his personal lawyers as attorney general, ordered the Department of Justice to pursue his political enemies, deployed the U.S. Marines to the nation's second largest city and leveraged the presidency to enrich himself and his family. He has demanded that comedians who mock him be fired, slapped his name on the Kennedy Center, pushed to seize control of elections, filed lawsuits against news organizations whose coverage he disliked and sued his own government seeking $10 billion in taxpayer money.

The president's actions have drawn comparisons to King George III, the British monarch whose rule inspired the American Revolution. Trump rejected this comparison in a CBS "60 Minutes" interview, stating, "I'm not a king. If I was a king, I wouldn't be dealing with you." However, when King Charles III visited Trump, the White House X account posted an image of both men captioned "TWO KINGS." The main resistance movement adopted the slogan "No Kings," with Ezra Levin of Indivisible explaining activists chose the label while thinking ahead to 2026 and the America 250 celebration. With a deferential Republican-controlled Congress, courts have become the last check on Trump, though his administration has sometimes defied their orders.

cards.headline: Missing diver found dead off Fort Pierce Inlet after search by Coast Guard and civilian friends
cards.teaser: The St.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is investigating after a missing diver was found dead on the ocean floor approximately 6 to 7 miles north-northeast of the Fort Pierce Inlet. The U.S. Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed 4 vessels to assist in the search. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit had independently monitored the Mayday call and was already en route to assist.

A group of civilian boaters who were friends of the missing diver departed the Fort Pierce Inlet at approximately 1 p.m., with aerial support provided by both the Coast Guard and FWC. Responding units made contact with the vessel involved nearly due east of Avalon State Park. At approximately 4:10 p.m., civilian divers entered the water and located the missing diver at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. Martin County Fire Rescue Lieutenant Daniel DeGrazia recovered the diver from the ocean floor. The diver was pronounced dead and transported to Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division is conducting the ongoing investigation.
